title: Two Hundred Fifteen Million
author: Harrison_Interactive
selftext:
Composer — "Composer by SoFi" — sells an AI that creates trading strategies and executes them, end to end, and advertises over $215 million of automated trades a day. Read their page closely and you will not find the step where the AI stops and asks you before a trade fires. We know what this class of AI does with a document it was supposed to read: we published the test. 20 of 60. 7 of 60. Evidence on none of it. A guessed blank in a chat window costs a wrong answer. A guessed blank inside an automated trade costs somebody their savings. Helena is built the other way.

https://harrisoninteractive.dev/news/2026-10-25-two-hundred-fifteen-million

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: a confirm button before every trade doesn't really fix it either. by the twentieth prompt people approve without reading. what holds up is splitting the keys: whatever writes the strategy shouldn't also hold the permission to open new positions.

replies.author: Harrison_Interactive
replies.body: Exactly — a confirm button just trains the click. By the twentieth prompt it’s muscle memory. The split holds up because it’s structural, not behavioral: whatever writes the strategy never holds the keys to open a position, and execution runs on the owner’s standing rules, not the model’s confidence. That’s how Helena is built, and it’s for this reason.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yep, keep the model's confidence out of the execution path entirely. that's how I set up Quantradin, which I made for this: an agent trades a fake-money US stock account, but opening a position needs a key its owner issues separately. free, quantradin.com

replies.author: Harrison_Interactive
replies.body:
Read your site, and the manual. Credit where it's due: real-spread fills and no look-ahead is more honest than most backtests ever get, and your desk keys are real separations.

But you told me the split holds up because it's structural. In your own manual, the strong version is opt-in. Don't scope the key and it's unrestricted. Approval mode is off unless the owner turns it on. And once a bot deploys, it runs the whole session without the user watching — your homepage calls that the design.

So by default, the AI that writes the strategy can also deploy it and run it. The writer can hold the keys, if nobody configures otherwise. Ours can't, in any configuration — there's no setting where the writer gets them, because they were never in the writer's hands to configure.

Last thing: all that architecture guards an account your FAQ says can't lose money, because there isn't any in it. The split earns its keep where the money is real.
